113344.etyen:
Borrowed from either Dutch fok (“foresail”) or Middle Low German, attested as vock, vocke (“foresail; puller”); the original sense was probably “puller”.
Dutch fok (“foresail”) is from Middle Dutch focke (“foresail”), of uncertain further origin. It has been tentatively connected with Middle Dutch vocken (“to blow”) and Proto-Germanic *fukkōną (“to blow, gust”).
Compare the parallel borrowings Norwegian Nynorsk fokk and Danish fok (“foresail, jib”). / Inherited from Old Norse fok (“drift; something blown through the air”), related to fjúka (“to drift, be blown away”) and fyke (“to fly or drift through the air”).
The related Old Norse verb fjúka continues Proto-Germanic *feukaną (“to blow; be blown away”), which has been derived from Proto-Indo-European *pewg- (“to billow, bulge, drift”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk fokk and Icelandic fok (“drifting”).

1000640.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Kazakh Қазақстан (Qazaqstan, “Kazakhstan”). The Kazakh name was coined from қазақ (qazaq, “Kazakh”) + -стан (-stan, “land, country”), literally “land of the Kazakhs”. The suffix -стан (-stan, “land, country”) is ultimately from Persian ـستان (-stân, “place, land”).
The ethnonym қазақ (qazaq, “Kazakh”) was originally used as a social designation and later became the name of an ethnic group. Its deeper etymology remains disputed.
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Kasakhstan, Danish Kasakhstan, Swedish Kazakstan, German Kasachstan, Dutch Kazac

1001152.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse drit (“excrement, filth”), from Proto-Germanic *dritą (“excrement”), a verbal noun related to *drītaną (“to defecate”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd- (“to have diarrhea”). Old Norse also had the masculine noun dritr (“filth, shame”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk drit, Icelandic drit, Faroese drit, dialectal Danish drit, dialectal Swedish dret, regional German German Driss (“shit”) and English dirt.
